title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
This page sets up the dynamical equation for a transversely vibrating elastic lamina (a cantilever clamped in a wall over the portion Aa). On the previous page Euler defined the deflection y = XY at abscissa x = BX and time t. He gave the curvature 1/R = (d²y/dx²), taken with x alone varying, so the bending moment is Kcc(d²y/dx²). Accelerations are measured in units of gravity: the fall height in one second is b, so g = 2b and the accelerative force is y_tt/(2b).

On this page he notes that y is a function of two variables. The problem therefore belongs to the part of integral calculus dealing with functions of two variables, i.e. partial differential equations. He says such problems need a quite distinct method if a complete and most general solution is wanted, recalling the vibrating-string controversy.

Section V: an element dx has weight (mass) K dx/k, with K and k fixed by earlier definitions, presumably the weight and length of a reference piece. Multiplying by the accelerative force (1/2b)y_tt gives the moving force (K dx/2bk)(∂²y/∂t²) in direction YV. If such forces acted on every element they would produce exactly the assumed motion. For the motion to be real, these elementary forces must be equivalent to the forces actually acting on the lamina. The only such forces are those exerted by the wall on the embedded part.

Section VI begins what the next page completes. The wall forces reduce to two forces at A and a. Reversing the inertial forces turns the problem into a static equilibrium problem (d'Alembert's principle). The equilibrium will lead to the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, in modern form EI y_xxxx + ρA y_tt = 0. This page itself contains only the setup.
errors: No mathematical errors. The units are consistent: force = weight × (acceleration/g) with g = 2b. Mass and weight are conflated, as was usual at the time, but this is harmless because gravity is the unit of force.

ideas.what: Expressing force as weight times acceleration/(2b), using gravitational units (b = fall distance in one second)
ideas.modern_name: Newton's second law in gravitational units
ideas.where_published: Throughout Euler's mechanics papers, e.g. E40 additamentum, E136/E177 era works

ideas.what: Recognition that beam vibration requires functions of two variables and partial derivatives (bracket notation), as with the vibrating string
ideas.modern_name: Partial differential equations / the 'general solution' debate
ideas.where_published: E119, E140 and later string papers; E443's introduction

ideas.what: Reversing the inertial forces to reduce the dynamic problem to equilibrium with unknown wall reactions at A and a
ideas.modern_name: d'Alembert's principle; clamped-end reactions (shear force and moment)
ideas.usually_credited_to: d'Alembert (1743); for beams, Euler and D. Bernoulli (1730s–1740s)
ideas.where_published: E443; similar reasoning in E40 (1744) and E526

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine setup of the beam-vibration problem via d'Alembert's principle. It is well documented in Truesdell's account of the rational mechanics of elastic bodies (Opera omnia II.11) and contains no unrecorded result.
transcription_corrections: The long s is consistently rendered as 'f' (e.g. 'folum' → 'solum', 'affumitur' → 'assumitur', 'manifeftum' → 'manifestum', 'fingulis' → 'singulis', 'maffula' → 'massula').
In the second force formula the image reads '2b.k' (or 2bk) in the denominator, consistent with the first formula '2kb'.
'Xy = dx' matches the image ('X y = d x'). It denotes an element of length dx at X/Y; it is likely a typesetting quirk for the element at Xx or Yy, not an equation.
